devtaHint:
At the very heart of every space lies a quiet, powerful centre; an unseen pulse from which all movement, harmony, and life seem to radiate. This is the Brahmasthan, the central zone of nine divisions, where the Deity of all deities, Brahma, resides. 

It is the very beginning of the Vaastu Purusha Mandala, emerging from the expansion of the Brahma Bindu, the sacred intersection of the Yama Sutra and the Brahma Sutra. From this single, potent point, energies unfold - spreading as triangles in Tantra and as squares in Vastu Shastra. In Tantra, this appears in the form of energy patterns like the Sri Yantra with its 45 triangles. In Vastu Shastra, the same energy expresses itself as an assemblage of 81 squares containing 45 deities.

Brahmasthan holds within it the essence of creation, preservation, protection, and restoration. It works as a transformer of cosmic energy, silently distributing vitality throughout the structure. It contains the subtle seeds of planets, elements, and deities the blueprint of all universal forces in their miniature form.

In Vastu, this sacred centre is also known as the Brahmasthan; the navel of any place. Just like a seed s empty space holds the potential to sprout, this central point carries unmanifest energy from which creation begins. Ancient Vedanta describes it as pure, unmanifest energy, and modern understanding echoes the same truth.

This centre nourishes the entire Vastu, much like a placenta supports a foetus through the navel. When the Brahmasthan is clean, open, and filled with positive vibration, its blessings spread naturally through the entire structure. Work begins to feel smoother, nature seems supportive, and life flows with cooperation and ease. A person connected to an auspicious Brahmasthan often feels energetic, joyful, and inspired. Their mind becomes sharp, capable of subtle thought, deep study, and genuine expertise.

However, when the Brahmasthan is disturbed, its imbalance sends ripples throughout life. Defects here can lead to serious concerns, including issues related to the heart, navel, and stomach, along with obstacles in progeny. Anything heavy, like beams, columns, stairs, or iron furniture, blocks its flow. Toilets, septic tanks, dirty water pits, pipelines, or dark colours further disrupt its purity. Unevenness, dirt, bad smells, breakage, lack of ventilation, and even making this zone higher than the surrounding rooms are all considered major defects.

The deity presiding over this sacred point, Brahma, mirrors this profound creative essence. His initial colour is golden or red - alive, warm, and luminous later turning into serene white. His swan symbolizes refined discrimination, the ability to separate the essential from the non-essential. His four arms embody the four directions, while his four faces represent the four Vedas: Rigveda in the East as the foundation, Yajurveda in the South as action, Samaveda in the West as rhythm and order, and Atharvaveda in the North as practical manifestation. The Akshamala in his hand represents calculation and wise management of resources, while the Kamandal signifies the reservoir of those resources. His deer skin, white and black, reminds us of the balance between dualities. Known also as Vidhi, he is the divine law-maker who sets creation into motion.

When the Brahmasthan is respected, the entire dwelling becomes a living, breathing sanctuary. When neglected, the entire system suffers. Caring for this centre is not merely a ritual - it is an act of honouring the soul of the space.

Remedies (Upay):

  Firstly, remove all defects like dirt, breakage, or bad smells.
  Perform a Havan (fire ritual) at least once a year, including Vastu Shanti.
  Offer white lotus, kheer, cow's milk, ghee, honey, and puffed rice (laja) in the Havan.
  To infuse positive energy, bury an auspicious symbol-engraved Manjusha (box) containing gems, herbs, minerals, gold, and mercury beneath the earth in the Brahmasthan.
  Sprinkle fragrant water daily (mixed with sandalwood, saffron, lotus).
  Install Pustaka (book), Shravaka (listener), Akshamala (rosary), and Kamandal (water pot) underground at an auspicious time.
  Place a swan (Hansa) and Kamandal in the center.
  Burn Guggul and Kapoor (camphor) daily.
  Use white and light colours.
  Establish Panchashirsha.
  Use red colour to activate dormant work and Kumkum in this area for benefit.

Remedies (Specific Items):

Gold, semi-precious stone (Dhatur), Tulsi. Hansa (swan), Kamal (lotus), Kamandal, Akshamala (rosary) as idol/image. 

Guggul, Kapoor (camphor). Golden color. Kheer, cow milk, ghee, honey, dhani for food and Havan.

In the gentle rhythm of the universe, there is a quiet force that holds, supports, and sustains much like the unseen strength beneath our feet. This protective presence is known as Bhudhar, the one who carries the earth. It is the energy of Lord Anant, Lord Vishnu, or Sheshnag, symbolizing foundation, stability, and the basic principle upon which life rests. In the cosmic layout of Vaastu, this deity occupies six divisions of the northern zone, close to the Brahmsthanam, strengthening the very core of a space.

Bhudhar reflects the essence of order, discipline, and the natural speed of life. With mythological Lord Vishnu as its guiding force, this zone holds the power of manifestation and the flow of regular activities. It is associated with protection, preservation, and restoration - qualities Vishnu embodies through his five powers: creation, preservation, destruction, grace, and bondage. The presence of Goddess Lakshmi at his feet emphasizes the connection of this zone with wealth, prosperity, and valued possessions. This is why the northern divisions governed by Bhudhar are ideal for keeping money, jewellery, important papers, and anything precious that requires safety and stability.

The nature of this zone is filled with Aakash (space), Prakash (light), and Urja (energy). These qualities accelerate movement and allow energies to flow in a circular, harmonious manner. But when influenced by heavy earth-related elements such as harsh solidity, excessive weight, or stagnation, the water element of this zone becomes absorbed and weakened. Any disturbance in this division is considered significant - if a fault from the periphery reaches Bhudhar, it turns into a severe Mahadosha, affecting both stability and prosperity.

When Bhudhar is auspicious, everything begins to move smoothly. Work evolves dynamically, grows naturally, and remains well-supported. The person feels protected from failures, guided by clarity, and grounded in determination. Their mind becomes strong and focused, able to stay with one goal without distraction. Knowledge deepens, creativity blossoms, and the individual reaches the peak of their field. Happiness flows in the home, bringing joy related to children, grandchildren, and wealth. Even external positions like Bhallat, Soma, and Aditi respond with supportive results. This becomes a place of happiness, where one enjoys worldly pleasures without becoming bound by them.

But when Bhudhar is disturbed, the story changes. The mind loses control, becomes swayed by illusion, and follows desires without discipline. Instability grows, goals keep shifting, and addictions may surface. Courage weakens, leading to financial loss and unnecessary waste. Lack of deep study or concentration prevents wisdom from taking root. The environment becomes clouded with negative energy, broken items, surgical objects, dirt, toilets, iron gates, and poor ventilation all contributing to imbalance.

The iconography of Bhudhar reflects this deeper truth. In Samarangana Sutradhara, Bhudhar is Anant, the infinite serpent. In Aparajita Prashcha, he is Lord Vishnu, whose dark colour symbolizes Maya, the great illusion. His clothes represent the thin line between ignorance and knowledge. His forest garland shows the bonds of worldly life, while the radiant Kaustubh jewel signifies knowledge shining through. Vishnu s vehicle, Garuda - the mighty bird, symbolizes the mind. When Bhudhar is strong, the mind is powerful, focused, and free of distraction.

When this northern division remains without faults, it supports wealth, fortune, and every form of prosperity both material and spiritual. It helps the occupant rise, freeing them from negative tendencies and strengthening their inner discipline. Symbolically, keeping a silver lotus or golden conch activates the positive qualities of this zone, honouring Lord Vishnu s protecting presence.

Remedies (Upay):

  Remove defects like dirt or broken items.
  Install Neelam (blue sapphire) and Pasha (noose) and Ankush (goad) under the earth at an auspicious time.
  Place the symbol of a plough (Hala) under the earth.
  Offer ghee and milk and Durva grass in Havan.

Remedies (Specific Items):

  Panna (Emerald). Kamal (lotus), Pasha (noose) as idol/image. Red color. 
  Kheer for food and Havan.

In the quiet glow of the eastern light, there is a zone in the home that carries the grace of honour, wisdom, and guidance. This serene space is ruled by Aryama, described as superior - one who stands apart with dignity, experience, and ethical strength. 

Aryama represents the essence of honourable conduct, dependable advice, and mature thinking. In the Vaastu Purusha Mandala, this deity occupies six divisions of the eastern zone, close to the Brahmsthanam, allowing his energy to blend with the central life-force of the structure.

Aryama is the ocean of Prana that nourishes Vivasvan, the ancestral energy or Pitru Kosha of the house. This is why the activation of Aryama becomes important when one wishes to pacify Pitru Dosha or when ancestral harmony needs support. 

The literal meaning of Aryama includes  close friend,   play fellow,  and  companion  a gentle reminder that this zone strengthens relationships, companionship, and emotional honesty. In Hindu tradition, the marriage oath is taken in the presence of Aryama, which is why this division plays a vital role in reducing disharmony between couples and restoring mutual respect.

This place is ideal for honourable, senior, and experienced individuals whether in a home or workplace. For policy-makers, planners, and administrative leaders, this is the zone that supports ethical decisions and clear direction. In a household, it becomes the appropriate place for senior family members. Its energy is equally suited for a place of worship, a study room, or a treasury, and it is especially auspicious for professions linked with righteousness or rules, such as legal advisors, lawyers, constitutional experts, or HR professionals.

When Aryama is auspicious, it fills a person with enthusiasm, respectability, and a refined way of living. Such individuals become pure in intention, civilized in behaviour, and naturally honourable. They radiate a quiet strength that others trust and follow. An auspicious Aryama also provides proper guidance, much like Surya s charioteer Arun who determines the direction of the chariot of light. Arun represents a teacher, a guide, and a creator of good deeds, qualities that begin to reflect in the person who benefits from this zone s balanced energy.

But when Aryama is disturbed, the person begins to lean toward deceitful behaviour, lies, disgrace, and habits that lack dignity. Their actions lose foresight, rushing toward quick fixes rather than thoughtful decisions. Structural defects such as broken walls, damaged flooring, faulty windows, or problematic doors in this zone further amplify negative effects, weakening clarity and trust.

The Vedic tradition identifies Aryama as the chief of Pitru Loka, the realm where ancestors dwell before rebirth. This emphasizes the deep ancestral connection of this zone. Activating Aryama with the correct methods, such as placing red coral beneath the flooring at the centre of these six divisions, awakens the fire element linked to Mars. This fire energy stirs the ocean of Prana here, restoring movement, clarity, and balance.

When Aryama is honoured, the home becomes a space of trust, direction, companionship, and ancestral blessings. When neglected, confusion and instability quietly take root. The key is to allow this eastern zone to breathe, shine, and guide just like the first rays of the morning sun.

Remedies (Upay):

  Remove defects and fill the area with positive energy.
  Place an OM symbol made of gold.
  If used for administrative purposes, place a golden staff (dand).
  Offer edible fruits, Urad dal, and sesame in Havan.
  Sprinkle fragrant water and use light colours.
  Install Munga (coral) under the earth with proper rituals.
  Use red and vermilion (sindoori) colours for creation.

Remedies (Specific Items):

  Gold. Sesame, Munga (coral). Dand (staff), Om symbol as idol/image.
  Urad, Sesame for food and Havan.

In the radiant warmth of the southern zone lies the powerful presence of Vivswan, one of the twelve names of the Sun; awake, alert, vigilant, clever, and wise. He is the promoter, the change controller, the one who illuminates direction and brings clarity to life. Scriptures also know him as Arun, the charioteer of Surya, the guiding force who leads the chariot of light toward its destined path. 

Positioned in six divisions of the south, close to the Brahmsthanam, Vivswan becomes the vital phase between the eastern Aryama and the western Mitra, holding within him the transformative journey of light.

Vedas describe Vivswan as the first to learn Yoga, born in the Raghu lineage, and a chief among the twelve Adityas. He connects the realm of Surya-loka with human life, protecting from the shadow of Yama. In Yogic tradition, he is the living and predominant deity on the Sun. These six southern divisions act like a shield standing between the soul s present journey and the path of Yama, guarding life, vitality, and the forward movement of one s destiny.

When this zone is charged with positive energy, the qualities of Vivswan shine brightly within the individual. The person naturally embodies Yamas and Niyamas self-control, truthfulness, non-violence, non-stealing, celibacy, and non-possessiveness. Life begins to flow in the right direction, decisions align with clarity, and efforts bear fruit. Such a person becomes wise, intelligent, long-lived, and healthy. They gain expertise in their field, and the capacity to teach and guide others comes effortlessly. Their life force is strong, their enthusiasm stable, and their direction clear.

But when the Vivswan zone is disturbed, the inner light flickers. Qualities like greed, dissatisfaction, fear, unrighteous behaviour, and lack of discipline begin to surface. One becomes directionless, frequently shifting goals, uncertain and unstable. Doubt, illusion, and lack of discretion cloud judgment. The person may feel tired, discouraged, or deprived of vitality, with declining courage and weakened health. Excessive pursuit of material desires, violence, and unhealthy impulses further pull the mind away from clarity. Diseases, suffering, or near-death-like conditions can appear when this zone becomes deeply imbalanced.

This zone is best suited for the seating of the main person in an office especially when facing south. It is also auspicious for the entrance in the south direction, or as a study room in other directions. Granaries and vehicles find positive influence here as well.

To maintain balance in Vivswan s domain, natural light is essential. Removing negative or stagnant items brings vitality back into the space. This should never be a place for servants or water elements, though water vapor may be generated if needed. For administrative areas, placing a lion symbol beneath the earth strengthens the force of Dharma. Symbols such as a mace (Gada), spear (Shula), power (Shakti), and noose (Pasha) may also be placed under the earth to support authority, protection, and clarity. Jatamansi oil applied to the head calms the mind and aligns it with solar vibrancy. Honey and rice should be consumed, and the same offered in Havan. Activation of this zone is also done by seeding the gemstone associated with Ketu, which cuts the unnecessary desires that bind the soul and elevates one toward Surya-loka, the realm of Vivswan.

The iconography of Vivswan reflects his luminous authority. He is the son of Aditi, father of Manu-Vaivasvata and Yama, and the creator of Dharma Shastra and Smriti Granthas. His wife is Saranyu, and his children include Yama and Shani, while his attendants are Dand and Pingala. His colour is red, his clothes sindoor-coloured, and a lion stands by his side, symbolizing Dharma. His four sons are Revant, Yama, and two Manus each carrying forward the light of his lineage.

This southern zone becomes especially sacred during Shraddh rites. One should sit in the Brahmsthanam, face south, and perform the rituals in this Vivswan division, allowing the ancestors to ascend to Surya-loka the radiant realm governed by Vivswan.

Remedies (Upay):

  Ensure natural light in the Vivswan zone.
  Remove negative energy items.
  Do not use this area for servants or stagnant water.
  If the room is used for administration, place a lion symbol (Simha) under the earth.
  Use Jatamansi oil for head application.
  Place symbols of mace (Gada), spear (Shula), power (Shakti), and noose (Pasha) under the earth.
  Consume honey and rice. Offer honey and rice in Havan.

Remedies (Specific Items):

  Gold. Sesame, Cat's Eye gemstone (Lahsuniya). Goad (Ankush), noose (Pasha) as idol/image. White color. 
  Sesame, rice, curd for food and Havan.

In the gentle expanse of the western horizon, where the Sun sinks into stillness and the day begins its quiet retreat, there lies a zone governed by Mitra, the cosmic friend and helper. This is the energy that supports, cooperates, and harmonizes. Mitra is the force that allows life to unfold with assistance rather than resistance. 

In Vastu, where the ultimate aim is to gain nature s cooperation, Mitra becomes the very heart of that intention. These six divisions of the west, positioned close to the Brahmsthanam, hold the essence of companionship, motivation, and alignment.

In the Vedas, Mitra and Varuna are often spoken of together as twins; Mitra, the cosmic priest, and Varuna, the cosmic royal power. Together they maintain the order of the sky, guiding the rhythm of day and night. Though beyond the hierarchy of the Sun, planets, or sky, they regulate the Sun s course itself. Mitra influences the sunrise, while Varuna presides over the evening. Savitr complements Mitra in defining the Sun s path. When Agni is kindled before dawn, it strengthens Mitra, showing the deep interdependence of these cosmic forces. These deities wield secret knowledge, through which they move the Sun across the heavens or cloak it with clouds. This power makes Mitra and Varuna among the most influential deities in the Vaastu Purusha Mandala.

When the Mitra zone is auspicious, cooperation arrives naturally people, money, resources, technology, and helping hands come forward without effort. One receives correct advice and guidance. The mind becomes wise, discerning, and capable of making the right decisions. Support flows from partners, especially the wife, bringing happiness, fame, wealth, and good fortune. This zone strengthens enthusiasm and makes a person feel like the owner of land, buildings, or factories blessed with long life and the respect of others. Assistance from government departments and servants becomes effortless.

But when this zone is disturbed, the harmony between Mitra and Varuna breaks. The balance between priestly wisdom and royal power collapses, creating disorder in life and relationships. Cooperation withdraws. Colleagues, servants, partners, and even children become uncooperative. Decisions turn weak and misguided. Bondage to illusion increases. Despite efforts, fame remains out of reach. Disputes arise, sometimes escalating into legal complications. Work moves painfully slowly what should take a day drags into weeks or months. Wealth slips away, enthusiasm fades, and life feels dull. Negative thoughts take over, leading to fear, confusion, and lack of clarity. In some cases, reproductive disorders may arise. Troubles from government departments further disturb peace.

This zone is suitable for study rooms, bedrooms, meeting halls, drawing rooms, or living rooms. In a west-facing house, this area becomes an excellent place for social gathering spaces. If needed, a water feature can be placed here.

To restore balance, Mitra s zone must be energized with purity and positivity. Removing dirt, broken items, and unpleasant smells clears the stagnant energy. Offerings of ghee, milk, and Durva grass in Havan uplift the space. Neelam (blue sapphire) can be installed beneath the earth with proper rituals, along with symbols like the noose (Pasha), goad (Ankush), and plough (Hala). These strengthen Mitra s cooperative nature and bring back order, stability, and observance the three virtues deeply associated with this deity.

When honoured, Mitra becomes the sustaining friend of both mankind and divine beings. When neglected, harmony dissolves. But with proper activation, this western zone becomes a fountain of support a quiet but powerful companion guiding life toward stability, grace, and success.

Remedies (Upay):

  Energize the zone with positive energy.
  Remove dirt, broken items, or bad smells.
  Offer ghee, milk, and Durva grass in Havan.
  Install blue sapphire (Neelam) under the earth with proper rituals.
  Place noose (Pasha) and goad (Ankush) under the earth.
  Install a plough (Hala) symbol under the earth.

Remedies (Specific Items):

  Durva (grass). Blue sapphire (Neelam). Noose (Pasha), goad (Ankush) as idol/image. 
  Ghee, milk, Durva for food and Havan.

In the serene and sanctified expanse of the northeast, where divinity feels closest and creation quietly stirs, lies the gentle yet powerful presence of Aap - the deity of water, peace, healing, and conception. The scriptures identify Apa with Uma or Uma-pati, Lord Shiva. Uma represents splendour and light, while Shiva embodies stillness and supreme consciousness. Together, they bring forth harmony, clarity, and the soft radiance that gives birth to new possibilities.

Aap is the very water element of the northeast - the divine water of the Ganges itself. This water is not merely physical; it is the sacred flow of grace surrounded on all sides by powerful deities. Diagonally lies Isha-Shikhi, the divine fire, continuously energizing this water with purity and illumination. Close by is Parjanya, the gentle shower of celestial blessings, followed by Jayant, son of Indra, connected to limitless sources of water. Aryama, the ocean of Prana, flows next. The holistic force of the Brahmsthanam lies diagonally below, grounding this sacred flow. There is also connection to Bhudhar, Lord Vishnu, the preserver, and to Aditi, the mother of all celestial beings. Together, these divine presences empower the Aap zone with unparalleled purity, healing, and creative potential.

When this zone is auspicious, life gains peace, stability, and cooperation. The mind becomes calm, steady, and content. One feels supported by friends, partners, and well-wishers. It enhances mental peace, emotional balance, and harmonious relationships. With the blessings of Aap and Apvatsa, creation begins whether it is the start of a new life, a new idea, a new relationship, or a new beginning. This sacred position influences the entire outcome of the northeast (Ishan). It is deeply linked with conception and the possibility of a female child. An auspicious Aap zone becomes the quiet doorway through which all good things gently enter.

But when this area becomes inauspicious, the mind loses its anchor. Instability, shifting desires, confusion, and frequent changes in goals cloud one s clarity. Cooperation disappears. Relationships weaken. Obstacles block marriage or delay the arrival of children. The healing force of this zone diminishes, and with it the ability to face challenges with strength. When imbalanced, Aap loses its soothing power and may even destroy the very healing energy that it naturally offers.

This zone is suitable for water features, medicines, or areas for assistants or less important tasks. A water place here can be especially beneficial, as it aligns with the true nature of Aap.

To restore harmony, this position must be made auspicious. Water is the key pure, flowing, and alive. Daily bathing with turmeric water on Mondays softens mental turbulence and awakens inner peace. Moong and rice should be consumed, and the same offered in Havan. Placing a goad (Ankush) beneath the earth supports stability and direction. These small rituals calm the mind, strengthen relationships, and remove obstacles to marriage and conception.

When honoured, Aap becomes a gentle ocean of healing, peace, and divine support. When neglected, its soothing power recedes. But through simple, mindful activation, this northeastern water returns to its natural state pure, luminous, and quietly transformative.

Remedies (Upay):

  Make the position auspicious to remove obstacles in marriage.
  Create a water place.
  Bathe daily with turmeric water on Mondays.
  Consume and offer moong and rice in Havan.
  Place goad (Ankush) under the earth.

Remedies (Specific Items):

  Pearl (Moti). Goad (Ankush) as idol/image. White color. 
  Turmeric, moong, rice for food and Havan.

In the gentle, cooling embrace of the northeast, where ideas are conceived and life force quietly awakens, lies the subtle yet powerful presence of Apavatsa. The term Apa means water, fluid, life-giving, adaptable, and in this sacred zone it symbolizes all forms of resources: people, wealth, equipment, opportunities, and the energy required to turn ideas into reality. If Aap is the divine water that inspires creation, Apavatsa is the force that carries those ideas forward into practical manifestation.

This is the location where life force takes its first movement. It is no surprise that Apavatsa is associated with Parvati, daughter of Himavan, the mountain of ice and water. Her presence symbolizes purity, nurturing, and the quiet strength needed to transform potential into creation.

When Apavatsa is auspicious, resources flow effortlessly. Individuals, money, tools, and support appear at the right time. The person gains inner strength the will to act, the energy to move, and the capability to perform. A beautiful state of oneness develops, where the mind becomes uniform, stable, and non-differentiating. In such clarity, one can understand any subject deeply, fully, and with natural ease. The capacity to build, create, or execute becomes strong. Ideas do not remain ideas under Apavatsa s blessing, they take shape.

But when this deity becomes inauspicious, the flow is disturbed. Resources dry up. Life force weakens. Health fluctuates and medicines lose their effectiveness. Plans falter, actions become delayed, and outcomes fall short of expectations. A person works but does not receive full results, leading to frustration and dissatisfaction. Obstacles in conception may arise, along with children-related issues. Even vision can be affected. The gentle life force of this region becomes unstable, affecting every form of implementation.

This zone is best suited for water bodies, cold storage, and activities needing cooling. It is also excellent for meditation, as it soothes the mind and brings clarity. Medicines kept here work effectively. Assistants or individuals handling less important tasks can be placed in this zone, as the water element promotes support and cooperation.

To restore harmony, the key is simple, remove defects and make the area auspicious. When purity is restored, Apavatsa resumes its natural function: transforming ideas into action.

Apaha brings the idea.
Apavatsa carries it into practical application.
Together, they form the divine cycle of creation.

Remedies (Specific Items):

  Pearl (Moti). Goad (Ankush) as idol/image.
  Milk, rice for food and Havan.

In the gentle brightness of the eastern sky, where the first spark of knowledge awakens, lies the sacred presence of Savitra - the source from which all understanding, wisdom, and creation begin. 

Savitra is identified with Vedmata, the mother of the Vedas, and with Savitri, the divine force behind knowledge itself. This is the place where pure insight originates, where the mind gains clarity, and where one learns to see things exactly as they are.

Savita is the source of all energies. When this energy flows toward material life, it is called Savitri. When it shines upon the spiritual path, it becomes Gayatri. In essence, Savitra is the mother-current of all illumination both worldly and divine.

When this zone is auspicious, a person becomes deeply knowledgeable, able to understand every aspect of a subject with precision and depth. Their discriminative power sharpens, allowing Vivek Shakti, the ability to distinguish truth from illusion, to flourish. Such an individual becomes proficient in multiple fields, follows their Swadharma (their own rightful path), and carries the purity of knowledge that allows them to perceive life clearly. This is also the zone connected with progeny and the beginning of any work. Just as knowledge is the seed of creation, Savitra becomes the point from which actions, ideas, and new beginnings take shape.

This zone holds the power of meditation. When balanced, it gives support, determination, and willpower. It is known to offer solutions for even the most difficult problems, making it a quiet source of inner guidance. The presence of Ganesh in this zone is considered especially auspicious, as it aligns with removal of obstacles and the beginning of auspicious work.

But when Savitra becomes inauspicious, obstacles rise, especially in progeny, or in starting new projects despite having planned meticulously. Work may stagnate, financial gains may be blocked, and unnecessary expenditure may drain resources. The natural flow of creation becomes delayed or weakened.

This area is ideal for those who discover and nurture hidden talents, whether in themselves or others. Students benefit greatly from this space, as do sons, research scholars, foremen, placement officers, or anyone whose role involves identifying abilities and bringing them to practical use. It is a place where new discoveries unfold, where curiosity strengthens, and where knowledge finds direction.

An auspicious Savitra zone becomes the cradle of clarity, creativity, and new beginnings. When honoured, it enlightens the mind and opens the path ahead.

Remedies (Upay):

  Food & Havan: Kheer and ghee.

Remedies (Specific Items):

  Yellow sapphire (Pukhraj). Lotus (Kamal), goad (Ankush), noose (Pasha), lion (Simha) as idol/image.

In the tender radiance of the eastern sky, where thought becomes clarity and clarity becomes action, dwells the divine presence of Savitra, the giver of knowledge, energy, and inspiration. 

Savitra is the mother of the Vedas, the place from which understanding first emerges, and the subtle force that awakens the mind to its true brilliance. When this same divine energy expresses itself for worldly growth, it is called Savitri; when it turns inward toward spiritual upliftment, it becomes Gayatri. All forms of awakening material, mental, or spiritual - begin here.

This zone holds the origin of knowledge, the spark of ideas, and the first stirring of creation. It represents the ability to grasp techniques, apply skills, and bring knowledge into practical use. Savitra is also associated with Hari, Lord Vishnu, the one who protects and sustains, reflecting continual movement, progression, and the ability to advance in both thought and action. The influence of Indra adds power, insight, and creative spark. Together, they form the intelligence and the drive behind all new work.

When Savitra is auspicious, a person becomes keenly knowledgeable, with sharp insight and pure understanding. They can see things as they truly are. Their discriminative power deepens, allowing them to make wise decisions and recognize their own hidden talents. They become proficient in multiple fields, follow their rightful path (Swadharma), and understand every aspect of any subject they study. Creative ideas flow naturally. Solutions appear with ease. Skill development becomes effortless. The person gains determination, willpower, and the strength that comes from meditation and inner clarity.

This zone is deeply connected to progeny and the origin of new beginnings. Just as knowledge gives birth to creation, Savitra influences the start of work, the birth of ideas, and the wellbeing of sons. It is also a space that reveals hidden abilities both in oneself and others.

But when Savitra becomes inauspicious, the light dims. Obstacles arise in progeny or delays in starting new projects. Plans do not progress. Efforts stagnate. Financial gains are delayed, and unnecessary expenditure increases. A person may fail to recognize their abilities or may recognize them but remain unable to use them. The mind becomes unstable, restless, and unable to find solutions or fresh ideas. Creative thinking fades. Confusion replaces clarity.

This zone is ideal for a study room, research area, skill development space, or any place where talents are trained and transformed. It is especially beneficial for students, sons, inventors, researchers, foremen, and placement officers anyone whose work involves understanding potential and converting it into success. The presence of Ganesh here is highly favourable, and the Shree Yantra brings additional strength. The Gayatri Mantra, dedicated to this deity, enhances its energy beautifully.

When honoured, Savitra becomes a fountain of creativity, clarity, and decisive action. When ignored, the ability to move forward quietly weakens. But once activated, this eastern light illuminates the mind, strengthens skill, and supports every new beginning with its divine brilliance.

Remedies (Upay):

  Food & Havan: Kheer and ghee, Offer Champaka flower and moong in Havan and consume them.
  Place symbols of noose (Pasha), lotus (Kamal), Kalpavriksha (wish-fulfilling tree), elephant (Gaja), and diamond (Hira) under the earth.
  Place these symbols visibly on the ground as well.

Remedies (Specific Items):

  Yellow sapphire (Pukhraj). Lotus (Kamal), goad (Ankush), noose (Pasha), lion (Simha) as idol/image

In the brilliant expanse of the northeast east zone, where clarity rises and the mind awakens, stands the radiant presence of Indra - the protector, the leader, and the force that destroys darkness so prosperity can unfold. Known as Vajri, Indra carries the powerful Vajra, the thunderbolt crafted from the bones of Rishi Dadhichi. With this divine weapon he destroyed Vritrasura, the demon of darkness and obstruction. Vritra symbolizes untimely interruptions, confusion, and stagnation, and Indra is the one who removes these shadows, bringing knowledge, growth, and forward movement. He is also deeply connected with Mann - the mind, its strength, direction, and brilliance.

When the Indra zone is auspicious, a person gains the rare ability to eliminate negativity from life. Their senses (Indriyas), thoughts, and desires come under healthy control. The mind becomes pure and focused, ready to move in the right direction. Such an individual becomes skilled in solving problems and gifted in offering wise counsel. They act with enthusiasm, clarity, and authority. 

Fortune supports them, and wealth flows with ease. Subordinates cooperate, administration favours them, and prosperity advances. Their intellect shines brightly, making them creators of wisdom, composers of scriptures, and sources of inspiration for others. Both spiritual and material growth flourish, and the personality begins to radiate with fame and brilliance.

But when this zone becomes inauspicious, the mind weakens. Desires and impulses begin to control behaviour. Decision-making becomes clouded, and problem-solving becomes difficult. One may act on wrong advice, feel unlucky, and lose enthusiasm. Subordinates stop obeying. Negative thoughts take over, disturbing both progress and peace. The strength that once protected and guided becomes scattered.

This zone is ideal for Vidya Kaksha - study rooms, skill development spaces, and places where the mind needs to think clearly or create new possibilities. It suits managers, controllers, administrators, principals, owners, and all master figures. In an east-facing home, this region is perfect for drawing or living rooms. It supports policy-making, treasury activities, meditation, study, Yagya, meeting spaces, and motivational discourses. This zone nurtures family stability, basic growth, and healthy thought processes.

Indra s iconography reflects his authority and abundance. His Shakti, Sachi, embodies Lakshmi the goddess of wealth. His vehicle, the elephant, symbolizes prosperity (Artha). The elephant s four trunks represent fortune, wise counsel, opulence, and enthusiasm. Indra appears with two arms, the Vajra in his right hand, standing as the luminous protector who destroys darkness and lights the path of progress.

Remedies (Upay):

  Offer Champaka flower and moong in Havan and consume them.
  Place symbols of noose (Pasha), lotus (Kamal), Kalpavriksha, elephant (Gaja), thunderbolt (Vajra), and diamond (Hira) under the earth, or keep them visibly above ground.
  Do not build a toilet here. Avoid items such as ashes, coal, straw, iron, or debris. Keep the place well lit with natural light and air.
  Fast on Sundays.
  Bathe before sunrise daily and offer water to the Sun. Perform Surya Namaskar.
  Donate and consume items related to the Sun. Offer red flowers to God.
  Use Kumkum or add it to bathing water.
  Keep water in a gold or copper vessel overnight and drink or bathe with it in the morning.
  Consume Masoor dal.
  Consume and offer honey and Malpua on Sundays.
  Install a Swastik, Airavat (elephant), goad (Ankush), and thunderbolt (Vajra) made of gold under the earth.
  Place ruby (Manikya) under the earth at an auspicious time.

Remedies (Specific Items):

  Diamond (Hira). Noose (Pasha), lotus (Kamal), Kalpavriksha, elephant (Gaja) as idol/image. 
  Champa flower for food and Havan.

In the quiet strength of the northern-eastern, eastern arc, where clarity sharpens and power gathers itself into focus lies the subtle yet formidable presence of Jaya, also known as Indrajaya. This is the zone where the thought process of Indra can be manifested, and where the victorious force of Maheshwar, Lord Shiva, quietly unfolds. Jaya is connected to Ishwar, the supreme resolver, and carries the essence of one who defeats enemies, destroys obstacles, and rises above disease and adversity. The energy here belongs to Rudra - the form of Shiva that expresses pain, frustration, or inner turbulence, only to release and transform it into strength.

When this position is auspicious, an extraordinary brilliance surrounds the person. Their personality becomes attractive, radiant, and commanding. They gain the inner force to conquer challenges whether enemies, illnesses, or obstacles in their work. Their efforts lead to victory, and they rise to prominent positions, becoming capable of fulfilling their resolutions with determination. Wisdom flows effortlessly, and understanding deepens. Wealth, prosperity, and recognition follow naturally. Their presence becomes powerful, inspiring others, and establishing them as victorious in their field.

But when Jaya becomes inauspicious, the inner Rudra becomes loud. Pain, frustration, or suppressed emotions surface as crying, shouting, or intense reactions. Their nature may become fierce, fearful, or unstable. Capabilities weaken, confidence fades, and discriminative power diminishes. Decisions become difficult, and overthinking takes over. What should be a zone of victorious clarity turns into a space of internal struggle.

Since Jaya is associated with Shiva, this zone often aligns with activities of purification, mental clarity, starting new ventures, or undergoing training in disciplines requiring strength and discipline. It is a channel through which Indra s strategic intelligence and Shiva s transformative power combine, giving rise to victory not by force alone, but through wisdom and inner mastery.

When honoured and balanced, Jaya becomes the silent strategist within the place where resolve strengthens, clarity emerges, and success takes form. When ignored, its energy turns inward, creating turbulence instead of triumph. But once aligned, this zone becomes the pure force of victorious intelligence, guiding one toward accomplishment, clarity, and mastery.

In the airy, shifting expanse of the northwest, where movement directs destiny and winds carry change, resides the dynamic and protective presence of Rudra. This deity occupies four divisions of the northwest zone, close to the Brahmsthanam, holding within him the force that regulates, controls, and channels the flow of life. The scriptures identify Rudra with Ishana in the Samarangana Sutradhara and with Shankar in the Aparajita Prashcha. Shankar is the bringer of welfare, prosperity, and happiness, while Har is the one who removes pain, poverty, sorrow, and all forms of suffering. Together, they reflect the true essence of Rudra - one who eliminates darkness and restores peace.

Rudra is the storm, the wind, the roar of awakening. The literal meaning of his name is  the roarer,  and he is praised as the mightiest force of the night - fierce enough to destroy negativity, yet protective enough to guard the vulnerable. He is the physician of physicians, holding thousands of remedies and cures. In many traditions, he is described almost as a divine paediatrician, protecting and healing children. That is why the bedroom of an unmarried daughter is traditionally assigned here so she naturally receives the cosmic protection of Rudra.

In the northwest matrix of deities, he governs Rog, Nag, Paapyakshma, and Shosh deities connected to disease, decay, and imbalance. Rudra controls and neutralizes them, acting as a powerful shield. The Rudra Sukt describes him as the inner self of all gods a reminder of the depth, subtlety, and transformative power within this zone.

When this position is auspicious, a person becomes happy, content, secure, and prosperous. Pain, poverty, sorrow, and all forms of inauspiciousness are removed. They gain the power to receive, obtain, and utilize resources effectively. This is also the zone of skill where abilities sharpen and are used correctly. Emotional balance stabilizes. Ideas begin to flow. Day-to-day tasks are completed smoothly. The person becomes capable of sustaining activities without interruption, channelizing support exactly where needed.

But when Rudra becomes inauspicious, the winds shift harshly. Sorrow appears. Prosperity declines. Diseases related to breath and lungs may emerge such as weakness, respiratory disorders, swelling, or tumours. The life force weakens. Small issues start irritating the person, disturbing their emotional stability. Wealth, respect, and fame diminish. Time, health, and money get misused or wasted. Progress slows, then stops, and eventually falls backwards. Enemies may gain dominance. The natural flow of work becomes blocked, leaving the person frustrated and drained.

This zone is suited for a treasury (Dhanalaya), an armoury (Ayudhalaya), or the residence of someone involved in litigation. It is a good space for medicines, airtight storage, dance or music rooms, or for a subsidiary entrance that channels movement in a controlled manner.

The iconography of Rudra reveals his depth. His vehicle is Nandi, the bull, symbolizing Dharma - steadfast righteousness. The crescent moon on his head represents Kala (art and knowledge), signifying complete understanding. The Trishul, his trident, represents unmanifest power and the three Gunas: Sattva, Rajas, and Tamas. Yet Shiva stands beyond these in the Turya Avastha, the fourth transcendental state. His five faces: Sadyojata (earth), Vamadeva (water), Aghora (fire), Tatpurusha (air), and Ishana (ether) symbolize mastery over all five elements.

When honoured, Rudra becomes a channeliser of support, the controller of flow, and the protector who sustains daily activities with ease. When ignored, movement becomes chaotic. But when his zone is aligned, one gains the ability to complete work effortlessly - supported by the silent, powerful rhythm of the cosmic wind.

Remedies (Upay):

  Offer rice (Bhat) in Havan.
  Consume and offer barley (Yava) in food and Havan.
  Place cardamom (Ela) under the earth.
  Install a trident (Trishul) symbol under the earth.

Remedies (Specific Items):

  Blue sapphire (Neelam). Trishul (trident) as idol/image.
  Rice (Bhat) for food and Havan.

In the deep, powerful stillness of the north-western arc where winds shift their direction and inner strength gathers into a silent centre resides the mighty presence of Rajayakshma, also known as Rudrajoy, Maheshwar, and Ishwar. This is the zone where the fierce, transformative power of Rudra meets the majestic, sovereign force of Maheshwar - the Great Lord, the chief, the master, the emperor among deities. Here, the mind releases its inner cries, frustrations, and accumulated pain, clearing the path for clarity, control, and decisive action.

Rudrajoy carries the essence of  crying out  not as weakness, but as a release. When inner pressure dissolves, strength rises. This is why this deity is known as the Holder the one who stops an idea in the mind at the right moment, holds it steady, and prepares it for further implementation. Without this refined pause, thoughts become scattered; but with Rudrajoy s blessing, they gain form, direction, and purpose.

When this position is auspicious, a remarkable power awakens within the individual. They become omnipotent in their approach capable of fulfilling their resolutions with unwavering determination. Their knowledge deepens, their wisdom sharpens, and they begin to understand everything with clarity and precision. Wealth and prosperity follow naturally, because the inner structure becomes strong. Their discrimination remains clear, their decisions firm, and their capability steady. Support arrives and stays, because the foundation becomes stable.

But when this zone becomes inauspicious, the opposite emerges. Efficiency drops. Abilities weaken. The discriminative power becomes dull. A person becomes unable to make decisions, caught in excessive overthinking that exhausts their inner energy. Even when support arrives, it does not stay; opportunities slip away because the internal structure is unstable. The mind becomes restless, unable to hold ideas long enough for them to ripen into action.

Rudrajoy is identified with Durga, the powerful feminine force who destroys obstacles and protects the devotee. Her silent presence in this zone brings strength, grounding, and the power to endure challenges with resilience. When this zone flows harmoniously, it becomes a pillar of support, a stabilizing force behind every implementation, and the quiet authority that turns vision into accomplishment.

But when imbalanced, even good opportunities lose their longevity. Support comes but it will not last. Ideas spark but they do not complete. Plans begin but they stop midway. The holder becomes the breaker.

To honour this zone is to honour the strength behind every decision, the clarity behind every resolution, and the stability behind every success.

Remedies (Upay):

  Perform Havan with ghee and rice to remove defects.
  Place a trident (Trishul) under the earth.
  Use Guggul and camphor (Kapoor) for fumigation.
  Consume Urad dal (black gram).

Remedies (Specific Items):

  Blue sapphire (Neelam). Trident (Trishul) as idol/image. 
  Guggul and camphor for Havan, Urad for food.

In the luminous, sacred stillness of the Northeast where the sky opens widest and the first touch of divinity enters the home shines the blazing presence of Shikhi, the flame-like deity who crowns the Vaastu Purusha Mandala. This is the topmost corner of the Northeast, the zone where water meets divine fire, where consciousness meets cosmic light, and where the human mind meets the realm of the gods. 

Identified with Ishana, Shankar, and Har, Shikhi is the master, the ruler, the one proficient in all arts, all knowledge, all directions. His energy stands above and beyond guiding, purifying, and awakening.

Shikhi is the Shiva-Chakra, the crown chakra of the Vaastu Purusha. Just as the corona of the Sun burns hotter and brighter than the Sun s heart, this zone radiates a power even greater than the Brahmsthanam. It acts as the supreme passage between the outer orbit of the macrocosm and the inner orbit of the 45 deities of the Mandala. It is the purifying flame, the Jyoti, that energizes the cosmic womb of water in Aap and Apavatsa. Through its continuous touch of divine fire, this water becomes Teertha, sacred and cleansing, capable of dissolving all negativity.

The very name Shikhi comes from Shikha, the sacred tuft described in Hindu tradition as the connector between cosmic energy and the brain. This place is known as the Adhipati Marm Sthan or MastuLingam - the control point of memory, emotions, intelligence, and the unification of mental faculties. Medically, this corresponds to the occipital lobe, the visual-processing centre. In Yogic teachings, Shikhi is the realm of Vyapini and Yogini Shaktis energies that connect the being to the Shiva Chakra. It is where Ganga and Yamuna unite to form Sarasvati the invisible fourth dimension connected to Time and the Kaal Chakra. This is why Shikhi governs direction, time, consciousness, and the control of all other energy centres within the Mandala.

When this zone is auspicious, life becomes beautifully aligned. A person s desires are fulfilled. They rise as masters of their field capable, powerful, and wealthy. Their tasks never remain pending; they complete whatever comes before them with ease. Life becomes organized, systematic, and filled with clarity. They plan well, execute with precision, and succeed effortlessly. Leadership qualities emerge naturally. Their mind gains calmness, stability, and contentment. Foresight becomes strong. They become the ruler of their own destiny.

But when Shikhi becomes inauspicious, its intense energy turns chaotic. Cooperation disappears, mental peace breaks, and instability enters the mind. Desires keep changing, goals shift constantly, and confusion clouds thoughts. Obstacles in marriage appear. Sadness, lack of prosperity, and incomplete tasks become common. Since this zone holds the memory and visual-processing centre, imbalances here can cause eyesight issues, mental disturbances, and emotional instability. Heavy items kept here disturb the delicate flow of cosmic energy. A store room blocks the mind, an office entrance brings accidents and electrical problems, and a kitchen here sparks anger and frustration. A toilet in this zone can cause serious mental disturbances. Sitting here for long periods may lead to detachment or disinterest in life.

Shikhi s iconography reflects his regal potency: the bull Nandi, symbolizing Dharma; the crescent moon representing art, knowledge, and time; the Trishul signifying the three Gunas and the unmanifest force; and Shiva s three eyes that see truth in all worlds. Surrounded by red, gold, mercury, quartz, peacock feathers, Shami wood, and symbols of Shiva s power, this zone becomes a gateway to higher consciousness.

Above all, Shikhi is the third eye of Shiva, the cosmic flame that reveals truth, purifies negativity, and allows the mind to conceive profound, divine ideas.

Remedies (Upay):

  Remove defects, especially those linked to marriage delays, and encourage sleeping in this zone.
  Bathe with turmeric water on Mondays.
  Consume moong and rice.
  Offer moong and rice in Havan.
  Place a goad (Ankush) under the earth.

Remedies (Specific Items):

  Gold, mercury (Para). Shami wood. Quartz (Sphatik) bull, damru (drum), deer, peacock, peacock feather.
  Ghee, rice (Bhat), paddy (Shali) for food and Havan.

In the gentle, life-giving embrace of the Northeast just below Shikhi s blazing flame resides Parjanya, the rain-bearing deity, the nourisher, the giver of insights, and the one who blesses the earth with growth. 

Parjanya is the cloud-lord, the one who showers blessings as rain, the bestower of boons, and the quiet force behind fertility, nourishment, and abundance. In Vedic tradition, Parjanya is the younger brother of Pusha or the son of Rishi Kashyap, and in the Atharva Veda, Parjanya is the father of all beings, with Bhumi and the sacred cow Vasa as his consorts symbolizing earth, milk, nourishment, and the motherly essence of creation.

This deity occupies the second position in the Northeast matrix. Here, the grace of heaven gently descends onto earth. Whenever divine fire receives offerings in the Southeast Nabha, division where cooking releases aroma and sacred vapours, the gods become satisfied, and their blessings reach the Parjanya zone as showers of prosperity. This is why traditional Vaastu places the stove in Nabha: the fire, considered the mouth of the deities, feeds them so Parjanya may release abundance. Fire in the Southeast and water in the Northeast work like cosmic partners - one creating, the other nurturing. When this bond is strong, blessings flow.

Parjanya s energy is deeply tied to insight, meditation, fertility, victory, new beginnings, innovation, and the creation of new traditions. An auspicious Parjanya zone turns efforts into blessings. Resolutions bear fruit like the Kalpavriksha: the wish-fulfilling tree. Work becomes smooth through cooperation from nature, people, and technology. This is a nurturing (Poshan) zone: medicines become effective, healing improves, and evil forces weaken. This zone also blesses female fertility, often resulting in more daughters being born and giving boldness and strength to the women in the home.

An auspicious Parjanya brings clarity, blessings, and a calm contentment. One feels supported, creative, guided. It becomes one of the best zones for meditation, as insights arise effortlessly here. It suits water bodies, meditation spaces, bedrooms, offices, drawing rooms, assemblies, and even hospital rooms dealing with antidotes and poison treatment. Flora and fauna thrive here naturally.

But when Parjanya becomes inauspicious, the rains stop metaphorically and energetically. Efforts do not bear fruit. Desires remain unfulfilled, creating deep dissatisfaction. Fertility issues arise, particularly for women. A washing machine in this zone can block conception; a dustbin can cause cyst formation. A toilet here leads to endless efforts without results. A kitchen brings financial losses and mental frustration. Heavy items block insight; the entrance increases expenses. A store room creates mental stagnation; a toilet here causes emotional and mental imbalance.

This is a delicate zone: its energy is soft, gentle, and deeply connected to feminine forces. Balancing it restores emotional harmony, clarity, and abundance.

The iconography of Parjanya reflects nourishment and fulfilment. The frog symbolizes rain and fertility; the cloud represents blessings; the lotus reflects purity. Kakkol, sesame, sandalwood water, tree turmeric, and yellow tones enhance this zone. A mother-child photograph improves relationships, while a flower bouquet or fruit basket invites continuous abundance.

Parjanya is the rain bull. When he roars, the sound sets seeds of life in the womb of the earth. That sound is energy, vibration, and the beginning of all creation.

Remedies (Upay):

  Place frog (Medhak) or cloud (Megh) images.
  Bathe with tree turmeric (Daru Haldi).
  Sprinkle sandalwood water.
  Offer ghee and lotus (Kamal) in Havan, or ghee and rice.
  Consume Kakkol, sesame (Til), and Poori.

Remedies (Specific Items):

  Tree turmeric (Daru Haldi). Frog (Medhak), cloud image (Megh Chitra), lotus (Kamal), noose (Pasha) as idol/image. Sandalwood (Chandan).
  Ghee, rice (Bhat) for food and Havan.

In the serene, life-nurturing expanse of the Northeast; where divine water flows with wisdom and purity - resides Jayanta, the bringer of victory, achievement, and flawless performance. 

The very name Jayanta means victory, and in the scriptures, Jayanta is also identified with Kashyap Rishi, whose lineage gave birth to gods, demons, Gandharvas, Yakshas, and Nagas. From his conscious will, entire universes of beings emerged pure creation flowing out of pure intention.

This zone reflects the story of creation itself. When consciousness was Satoguni; pure, luminous, untouched - success followed effortlessly, simply through resolve. But as consciousness descended toward Rajas, external elements became necessary to assist the act of creation. Various energy fields developed, and the universe diversified. Jayanta preserves this memory of effortless success: when the mind is disciplined and the senses are controlled, victory becomes natural. This zone builds inner mastery, outer achievement, and the strength to carry out all tasks with excellence.

When Jayanta is auspicious, a person becomes focused, clear, and determined. Success follows their resolve. Their efforts bear fruit without struggle. Wealth, comforts, buildings, land, vehicles, children, grandchildren these blessings arrive with ease. They excel in meditation and deep study. Their ideas flow clearly, and their enthusiasm remains steady. The mind stays in control, and the personality becomes capable of understanding all aspects of life. This zone also teaches strategic intelligence Saam, Daam, Danda, Bheda the wisdom to deal with the world through peace, persuasion, discipline, or strategy when needed.

When the Jayanta zone is disturbed, the mind loses its direction. One becomes restless, unable to stick to one goal. Tasks are started but left halfway. Confusion increases. Wealth declines. Relationships with children and grandchildren weaken. Even professional coordination, between head office and branches, suffers. The person feels scattered, unable to bring their goals to completion.

This is a sensitive zone for the mind and emotions. A toilet here affects children: they become shy, struggle to express themselves, and remain overly simplistic. Heavy use of black colour or circular shapes disturbs the stability of this zone. A sword placed here may make one overly critical or harsh in speech. But when balanced, the same space promotes creativity, action, determination, and clear solutions.

Plant life thrives beautifully here, enhancing positivity. A wine bar or book collection brings social and intellectual enrichment. A bedroom here creates street-smart qualities. An entrance in the Jayanta zone equips the residents with all tools needed for worldly success, profits, prestige, and opportunities. Living and dining rooms do well in this zone, encouraging harmony and a forward-moving life.

Jayanta is also a quiet reminder of the turtle (Kachhua), symbol of steadiness and perseverance. Its presence here keeps the mind aligned with one goal instead of wandering.

When honoured, Jayanta becomes the inner strategist the achiever who sees clearly, decides firmly, and succeeds gracefully.

Remedies (Upay):

  Place moon (Chandrama), Jatihimgulya plant, umbrella (Chatra), ghee, and butter (Makhan) under the earth.
  Place a turtle (Kachhua) on the ground to remind one of the goal.
  Consume ghee and butter.
  Offer ghee in Havan.

Remedies (Specific Items):
  Moon (Chandrama), umbrella (Chatra), turtle (Kachhua). Cinnabar (Hingalu).
  Ghee and butter for food and Havan.

In the bright, ascending energy of the eastern perimeter - where clarity rises, where intentions take direction, and where authority awakens - resides Mahendra, the king of the gods, the lord of the senses, the ruler of heaven s forces. His name itself means Indra, the supreme deity of Svarga, the bringer of lightning, thunder, storms, flowing rivers, and the heavenly rains. Across Hinduism, Jainism, and Buddhism, Mahendra appears with the same luminous reflection: the one who governs natural powers that remain in rhythm with the laws of nature.

This is the fourth deity on the eastern perimeter of the Vaastu Purusha Mandala. Here, fire takes its most refined form; the fire that melts deep snow to release rivers, transforming earth-bound water into the blissful flow of the Ganges. 

Mahendra represents this positive, life-giving form of Agni. Whenever darkness, confusion, or obstruction threatens one s progress, Mahendra wields the Vajra the thunderbolt forged from divine sacrifice; to destroy those forces and restore prosperity.

When the Mahendra zone is auspicious, it becomes a seat of fortune, influence, brilliance, and leadership. A person receives correct advice and becomes an excellent consultant. Their personality becomes shining, their intellect pure, their enthusiasm high. Wealth and opulence flow naturally. Subordinates cooperate and follow willingly. Support from administration increases, and prosperity grows. They rise as rulers, controllers, administrators ideal for managers, principals, owners, policy-makers, and top decision-makers.

The person becomes both spiritually elevated and materially successful. They gain fame, recognition, and a place of respect. Their mind, senses, and intelligence remain in harmony. They inspire others, create knowledge, and embody the best qualities of Mitra, Varuna, and Agni all at once. This zone is ideal for study, Yagya, Veda recitation, meditation, conferences, and motivational work. In an east-facing home, it is highly auspicious for the main drawing room or living room. A bedroom here gives powerful connections; sleeping in this area refines temperament and choices. A living room here enhances social prestige and beneficial contacts. An office table and chair placed here elevate the occupant to top authority.

When Mahendra is disturbed, fortune fades. A person may act on wrong advice, remain unenthusiastic, or lose control over subordinates. Disobedience arises. Government-related troubles emerge. A toilet here destroys recognition efforts go unnoticed, and socially the family may be looked down upon. Certain disturbances can even lead males toward addictions involving alcohol, gambling, drugs, or imbalance of desires. Black colour, a Saturnine influence, creates heaviness and negativity here. But orange brings strength and upliftment.

Mahendra s iconography reflects the splendour he bestows. His Shakti, Sachi, embodies Lakshmi - the goddess of prosperity. His vehicle is Airavat, the white elephant with four trunks symbolizing fortune, guidance, opulence, and enthusiasm. Indra stands with two arms, the Vajra raised in his right hand, destroying the monsters that block prosperity. Activating this division with a silver Vajra symbol brings divine protection and removes ambiguity from life, melting inner darkness with the light of understanding.

When balanced, this is the zone of great associations, powerful contacts, luxury, and financial upliftment. When an Ashoka Pillar symbol is placed here in a balanced environment, the home receives government-related benefits. A beneficial entrance here becomes one of the most auspicious possibilities in Vaastu, ushering prosperity, opportunity, and a royal flow of life.

Mahendra is the kingly force that clears the skies, strengthens the will, removes obstacles, and crowns the individual with success.

Remedies (Upay):

  Do not build a toilet here. Avoid ashes, coal, straw, iron, or debris. Keep this region filled with natural light and fresh air.
  Fast on Sundays. Bathe before sunrise and offer water to the Sun. Perform Surya Namaskar.
  Donate and consume Sun-related items. Offer red flowers to God.
  Use Kumkum or mix it in bathing water.
  Keep water in a gold or copper vessel overnight; drink or bathe with it the next morning.
  Consume Masoor dal.
  Consume and offer honey and Malpua on Sundays.
  Install a Swastik, Airavat (elephant), Ankush, and Vajra made of gold underground.
  Place a ruby (Manikya) under the earth at an auspicious time.

Remedies (Specific Items):

  Vajra (thunderbolt), Airavat (elephant), lotus (Kamal). Jasmine (Chameli, Mogara). 
  Panjiri for food and Havan.

In the radiant heart of the eastern perimeter, where dawn opens its eyes and the world awakens, stands the luminous presence of Surya, the Founder, the Observer, the Awakener, and the true Executor of all beginnings.

Surya, also called Vivswan, is one of the twelve Adityas and the father of Yama and Shani, the keepers of cosmic law. He is Prabhakar, the one who illuminates everything, dissolving darkness with knowledge and awakening life with brilliance.

This central eastern zone is unique. Just as Yama, Varuna, and Soma occupy central power points in their respective directions, Surya holds the pivotal core of the East. With equal distance to both sides, this field carries the active stream of the Sushumna Nadi, the central channel that connects human consciousness with divine existence. This gives Surya an intense and independent power centre. Because Sushumna channels spiritual force and Pingala embodies fire energy, any direct entrance or overstimulation here activates both currents together. This frequently leads to heightened aggression, impatience, friction, and disturbances within the family.

Classical Vaastu therefore teaches a clear rule: entry from Surya s division provokes anger and harshness. This field should be approached gently along the clockwise path of reverence, never struck directly.

When Surya is auspicious, life gains direction and brilliance. A person becomes disciplined, impactful, energetic, and victorious. Their personality radiates authority and purity. The senses, mind, and intellect remain sharp. They gain the courage to face circumstances without retreat. Speech becomes truthful, action becomes firm, and both spiritual and material progress accelerate. Subordinates respond with respect. Such individuals inspire, lead, and become examples to others. Their observation deepens and their insight sharpens, for Surya governs the power of sight, clarity, and system management. As the guardian of the planetary forces, Surya stabilizes the home s energy and strengthens its central masculine force.

When Surya weakens, everything reverses. The person becomes dull, ineffective, and confused. Decisions are hurried and incorrect. Depth of understanding disappears. Lies, hypocrisy, and indecision begin to surface. Subordinates disregard instructions. Systems fail and order collapses. In households where Surya is weak, the men often become overly soft or lose initiative. When the head of the family feels unseen or unheard, this is the first zone to examine.

An entrance here can create short temper and aggressive behaviour. A kitchen here intensifies anger. A temple, however, causes no disturbance. Warm orange tones uplift this field; copper and brass representations of the Sun steady its weakened fire and restore balance to the male aura of the house. Images of Vishnu create harmony and stability.

This zone supports managers, controllers, administrators, principals, owners, or any role requiring leadership and systemic oversight. It is favourable for study, scriptural recitation, meditation, ritual, contemplation, and meetings. In an east-facing home, this becomes a graceful place for the drawing or living room. A bedroom placed here instills authority and refined temperament.

Surya s iconography reflects his radiance. His colour is red and his garments glow like sindoor. His attendants, Dand and Pingala, symbolise discipline and karmic record. The lion beside him represents Dharma. His four wives; Rajni, Rikshubha, Chhaya, and Suvarchasa, reflect protection, beauty, brilliance, aspiration, and energy. Arun, his charioteer, guides his seven-horsed chariot across the heavens, awakening every being to purpose and clarity.

Surya is the inner light, the guardian of order, the force of clarity, and the being who teaches that mastery arises only through conscious observation.

Remedies (Upay):

  Avoid constructing a toilet here and keep the space free from ashes, coal, straw, iron, and debris. Maintain brightness and natural ventilation.
  Observe a fast on Sundays. Bathe before sunrise and offer water to Surya. Practice Surya Namaskar.
  Donate and consume items associated with the Sun. Offer red flowers in worship.
  Apply kumkum or mix it in bathing water.
  Keep water in a gold or copper vessel overnight; drink or bathe with it in the morning.
  Consume masoor lentils.
  Consume and offer honey and malpua on Sundays.
  Install symbols such as Swastik, Airavat, Ankush, and Vajra made in gold beneath the earth.
  Place a ruby in the ground at an auspicious moment.

Remedies (Specific Items):

  Gold, Swastik, Airavat, Ankush as image forms; the colour red; 
  Honey and Malpua for consumption and ritual offering.

In the calm and discerning brilliance of the eastern and southeastern arc, where truth meets action and where purpose blends with daily life, rises the gentle yet immensely powerful presence of Satya, the keeper of authenticity, righteous conduct, clarity, and inner correction. Satya is the son of Dharma, and his essence is truth, trust, reliability, and integrity. This is the field where one honestly examines oneself, aligns actions with the right path, and builds goodwill that remains unshaken through time.

Satya is the field of conscience, the mirror where the mind sees its own intentions. It reveals the unfiltered truth of who we are when no one observes us. This field teaches the discipline of living with honesty, keeping commitments, and walking the right path even when it demands strength and sacrifice.

When Satya is balanced and auspicious, a person becomes deeply authentic and trustworthy. Their words carry clarity and moral weight. Their understanding becomes pure, allowing them to see situations exactly as they are. Such individuals develop the qualities of sacred discipline, selfless action, and generosity. They rise as excellent advisors, consultants, policy makers, legal experts, and judges. Their presence inspires trust and respect. Their conduct brings dignity to every space they enter.

But when Satya becomes weak or disturbed, the inner compass spins in the wrong direction. One begins to mistake wrong for right, illusion for clarity, and harmful choices for wise decisions. Intellect becomes corrupted. Judgement becomes unreliable. Obstacles appear at the very beginning of every task. Financial decline begins. Wasteful spending becomes frequent. Emotional life becomes heavy and uncertain, clouded by confusion and sorrow.

Satya is deeply connected with the idea of commitment, especially marital commitment, which is considered among the highest responsibilities in life. When this field is disturbed, a person may shift partners easily, commitments may break suddenly, and others may fail to honour their promises. In matters of marriage stability and trust, this is the first zone to examine. Mirrors here weaken clarity and distort truths. Strong blue tones reduce sincerity. Green is acceptable but must be used lightly and thoughtfully.

This field is ideal for chambers of decision makers, consultants, policy rooms, meeting spaces, drawing rooms, and study areas. Any place that demands clarity, fairness, and structured thinking thrives under the influence of Satya.

When Satya is honoured, it grants right judgement, consistency, reliability, and the strength to fulfil promises. When ignored, it shakes the foundation of trust and harmony in life.

Remedies for this field

  Keep the area clean and free from toilets, broken items, or clutter.
  Place a symbol of a sacred bull on the ground to stabilise the field.
  Offer clarified butter, wheat flour, and honey in sacred rituals and consume these mindfully.

Remedies (Specific Items):
  Rosary (Akshamala) and book (Pustaka). White color. Butter (Makhan) and coconut (Nariyal) for food and Havan.

In the quiet, reflective stretch of the southeastern southern mind-space, where thoughts begin to churn and inner sparks of desire take shape, resides the powerful energy of Bhrisha - the deity of analysis, ignition, stimulation, and mental churning. 

The very meaning of Bhrisha is  to churn,   to agitate,  or  to stir deeply,  much like the way an idea is born when the mind rubs two contrasting thoughts together. This field is identified with Kamadeva or Manmatha, the churner of the mind, and also with the fiery intensity of Krodha, or sharp, focused agitation.

Bhrisha is the zone where the mind tests itself, where thinking becomes sharper, ideas are scrutinized, and conclusions are forged with clarity. It is the inner workshop of reasoning where thoughts are filtered, polished, and shaped into decisions.

When Bhrisha is auspicious, the mind becomes a refined instrument. One can analyze subjects properly, distinguish right from wrong, and arrive at correct conclusions. Desires become aligned with knowledge, scriptures, and higher intentions. The mind stays focused on good goals; decisions are born from clarity rather than confusion. It becomes a zone of constructive thought and insightful evaluation.

But when Bhrisha is inauspicious, analysis becomes clouded. One misjudges situations, arrives at wrong conclusions, or wastes time and resources. The mind may overthink excessively - circling around problems without finding solutions - and the end results collapse under confusion. Execution of actions becomes difficult. Tasks begin but do not reach completion. Even small defects here can disrupt analytical abilities, leading to strict, harsh behavior in authority figures, anxiety, BP fluctuations, and continuous illness in elderly partners sleeping in this area.

This zone is ideal for contemplation, planning, observation, discussions, meetings, accounting, fault detection, machine repairs, and any activity that requires examining details. If thinking or analysis in a home or office is disturbed, or if decisions are consistently going wrong, this is the first place to check.

This is also the field of desire because desire is the spark that pushes the mind to think. When balanced, desires create progress. When imbalanced, they create agitation. Metallic showpieces, sewage, or harsh blue colour disturb this delicate energy. Dustbins may not always be favourable. A sewing machine can create anxiety. A mixer-grinder, interestingly, supports the symbolic churning energy. Placing Kamdhenu here enhances positive vibrations.

Balanced softly, this zone gives the strength to think clearly, understand deeply, and decide wisely.

Remedies (Upay):

  Remove defects such as negative energy, broken items, or dirt.
  Consume butter (makhan) and coconut (nariyal).
  Use coconut oil.

Remedies (Specific Items):
  Hartal (orpiment). Dark blue color. 
  Butter (makhan) and coconut (nariyal) for food and Havan.

In the gentle, ever-expanding stretch of the northwest sky-field where thoughts rise like wind, where space opens like a doorway into possibility, and where life breathes through its own invisible rhythm lives the subtle and powerful energy of Akash, also called Antariksha. This is the space between earth and heaven, the field of air, movement, bandwidth, market space, and inner expansiveness. It is the oxygen that allows all manifestation to happen.

Akash is identified with Vayu, the cosmic wind free, swift, boundless, and intelligent. Vayu carries Pranavayu, the vital air that sustains life. Akash is the subtle space that holds everything yet remains untouched by all it holds. It is the region where ideas take flight, where thoughts gather strength, and where life gains the momentum to move forward.

When Akash is auspicious, a person becomes energetic, wise, and intelligent. Their mind glows with a golden purity, quick and sharp like Garuda s flight. They do not tire easily. Contentment becomes natural desires stay under control, and greed does not take root. The mind remains steady, focused, and swift, able to think clearly and act gracefully. Their inner space widens, giving them the capacity to make room for expansion in life more growth, more possibilities, more markets, more audience, more bandwidth.

But when this zone is inauspicious, energy collapses. Fatigue becomes constant. Desires expand endlessly, never being satisfied. Greed, restlessness, and discontent dominate the mind. Health issues related to Vayu; pain, numbness, stiffness, begin to rise. The person becomes sorrowful, and life events begin to feel stuck. Delayed payments, delayed marriages, delayed decisions - any form of stagnation often points toward imbalance in the Akash zone.

In practical life, Akash is the field where recognition happens whatever you keep here gets noticed and appreciated. But a door in this zone may cause financial losses. A weak Akash increases the chances of theft. A store here blocks joyful events. This field also relates strongly to Venus, affecting females more when imbalanced. Cuts in this area often show the elder son drifting away from home or not being fully connected with the family.

A well-balanced Akash opens life like the sky; vast, free, and full of movement.

Remedies (Upay):

  Place Agaru (agarwood) under the earth.
  Use Agaru fragrance.
  Place symbols of Dand (staff) and Pasha (noose) under the earth.
  Consume Urad dal (black gram), Gud (jaggery), and turmeric (haldi). Offer these in Havan.
  Place Mahaneel and gold under the earth.
  Use Sarvaushadhi (all herbs), ghee, turmeric, and rice (bhat) for consumption and Havan.
  Place Kulthi (horse gram) under the earth.

Remedies (Specific Items):

  Agaru (agarwood), turmeric (haldi). Dand (staff), Pasha (noose) as idol/image. 
  Urad and gud (jaggery) for food and Havan.

In the vibrant, rising corner of the Southeast where fire awakens, actions ignite, and the whole Vastu gains its spark lives the powerful deity Anil, the subtle wind behind the flame. Though associated with Agni, Anil represents the wind within fire, the force that uplifts, accelerates, and carries intentions upward. He is the elevator, the uplifter, the energy that turns a mere spark into a blazing force of creation.

Agni, with whom Anil is closely tied, is portrayed as red-hued, with matted hair and smoke-coloured garments, surrounded by flames and carrying three eyes of perception. Agni means  the one who is ahead  a leader, an inspirer, an initiator. He moves first, shows the way, and becomes an ideal for others. 

Anil s presence at the very top of the fire corner shows how wind and fire are inseparable in their work. Fire cannot burn without air; fragrance cannot spread without the wind; rituals cannot reach the deities without the subtle movement of Agni carried by Anil. The smoke of fire is simply the closed form of the wind element.

This is why Anil is considered immensely important, he helps carry the aroma (Nabha) from the Southeast to Parjanya in the Northeast, completing the sacred circuit of blessings. Through Anil, the organic unity of all deities becomes visible.

When Anil is auspicious, a person becomes wealthy, joyful, opulent, and well-reputed. They follow Dharma naturally. Success comes with clarity and perfection.
